data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject when the test is installed as part of the same artifact that it tests, creating a self-referential loop where the test's own installation becomes a subject of the test. The 3-of-26 result is explained by compile.py's installation mutating the very guard definitions it was supposed to test, so that 1 of 9 mutations was lost because the guard that would have caught it was itself modified during shown-to-fail-first installation, while other modules had their guards installed before testing began.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The loss would be 0/9 if installation and testing were separated into distinct processes","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The loss would be 9/9 if every guard module were overwritten during installation","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect would not appear if compile.py were already installed before the mutation run","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The asymmetry between 1/9 and 4/4 to 6/7 would vanish if the installation order were reversed","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Installation under shown-to-fail-first causes compile.py to execute its own test harness during installation. This execution triggers a code path where the compiler recompiles its own guard modules. The first planted failure causes a partial recompilation that overwrites one guard's bytecode with an older version that lacks the mutation check. The 1/9 mutation that was lost corresponds to the specific guard whose bytecode was overwritten, while the other modules' guards remained intact because their installation order placed them after the failure-priming step.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
